title_en: Thoughts on the Memory Industry and Latest Developments
sections: The importance of memory in the AI era is still not fully priced in — it is the single most important strategic resource of the AI era — and I expect the valuation paradigm for leading memory companies to re-rate further. At the same time, my investment thesis on Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix needs further refinement (this is the third point below, and it's the core of my investment view), and I want to track the latest developments in the industry.
Core logic and latest industry developments

On the day SK Hynix listed its ADR, Chairman Choi introduced the concept of "Memory-as-a-Service" (MaaS) — an attempt to shift memory from a traditional commodity model to a software-style rental model, with the goal of changing the valuation paradigm for memory makers. My read is that this will probably stay at the level of a narrative and won't actually get implemented, for the following reasons.

First, memory is tightly bound to HBM or DRAM — renting a GPU inherently means renting the memory attached to it. "Memory-as-a-service" would only apply to idle, unused memory, but for technical and licensing reasons, memory can only be pooled and shared within a company's own data centers, and SK Hynix won't own its own data centers anytime soon.

Second, on the technical side, the latency introduced by CXL constrains the use cases for memory rental. My own caveat: I don't know whether a future breakthrough in CPO (co-packaged optics) technology could change this — I'll come back to this point below.

Third, MaaS itself doesn't make economic sense, especially while the memory supercycle hasn't cooled off. If you can sell memory at an extreme premium, there's no reason to rent it out instead — and that extreme premium comes precisely from the supply–demand imbalance. If supply and demand were balanced, why would a customer need to rent rather than just buy? The whole rationale collapses.

Finally, memory rental would cannibalize the memory makers' own core business, since it inherently eases the very supply–demand tightness that's driving today's pricing.

Taken together, MaaS is most likely just a narrative for now. But it does reveal how badly the memory makers want to escape the traditional cyclicality of their business — and a number of the points below reflect the same ambition, some of which I think are actually achievable.

The market has overreacted to the panic around CXMT and YMTC's listings and capacity expansion.

First, CXMT's product line skews toward consumer-grade parts and it has almost no share in advanced DRAM or HBM for AI data centers. Meanwhile the share of AI-data-center revenue at Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron keeps rising sequentially — per Micron's latest earnings, over 60% of its revenue now comes from AI data centers, and Samsung and SK Hynix, which have larger HBM share, are probably even higher.

Second, CXMT hasn't started a price war. When Apple approached CXMT for DRAM pricing, it found CXMT's prices were actually higher than the big three. That's arguably good news for the industry as a whole, since it means no player is breaking the current pricing discipline for now — on top of spot prices staying elevated, CXMT's own costs are higher because of yield issues, so it can't afford to cut prices anyway.

Third, CXMT does have a real technology gap versus Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix — including but not limited to lack of access to EUV, less accumulated process experience, a thinner talent bench, and weaker stacking technology. So its impact on the highest-margin pools for the big three — HBM and AI-data-center server DRAM — is limited for now.

Finally, CXMT's bit shipment growth may not be accelerating as fast as people imagine, though this is something that needs long-term tracking.

The supply–demand gap may be even more severe than people think. Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have all sold out their 2027 DRAM and HBM capacity — most buyers are only getting 60%–70% of what they originally requested. Micron's CEO says customers want roughly 50% more supply than it can commit to. SK Group's chairman says global memory supply could still be running about 20% short of demand through 2030. Samsung says the shortage will persist through 2028, with 2027 being even tighter.

In the past, my investment in Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix was really more of an industry-level bet — the view that memory has become the AI era's strategic resource. All AI hardware is fundamentally a byproduct of this AI supercycle, so if optical communications, optical interconnect, and liquid-cooling companies are getting extremely high valuation multiples, memory companies shouldn't be stuck with such low multiples. Re-rating the valuation model for memory is overdue, especially given the profit certainty that long-term agreements now provide.

On the company level, my thinking was that Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron are essentially the only three real players in this memory supercycle — CXMT is still too small to matter — and the barriers to entry are extremely high for any newcomer. On top of that, structural demand for memory is shifting, and so is the nature of the product itself: structural demand from AI data centers, robotics, and autonomous driving, combined with HBM's status as an extraordinarily difficult product that turns a commodity into something closer to a customized part. For all these reasons, I thought all three deserved to be owned. Samsung and SK Hynix had the lowest valuations and the largest HBM share — meaning their profits were likely to persist longer — and HBM is naturally tied to hyperscalers and the biggest tech giant of all (Nvidia), which gives them better earnings visibility and durability. That's why SK Hynix became my largest holding. Micron benefits from onshore US manufacturing, which largely shields it from geopolitical risk and arguably deserves a premium for that, so I also built a position in Micron. (My SanDisk position is based on a separate thesis, which I covered in an earlier single-name note.)

Honestly, I hadn't thought through my selection among these three companies all that clearly. I'm not a semiconductor specialist, and I can't guess who the eventual winner will be — my past process for these three names leaned mostly on valuation, HBM share, and management execution.

My view has shifted somewhat now. First, I don't need to guess who the winner is, because all three are probably winners. Samsung and SK Hynix's accumulated know-how in DRAM and HBM is very hard to displace; Micron is geopolitically indispensable to the US government and essentially can't be allowed to lose. So all three are likely winners, and the market is large enough to comfortably support three winners at once.

Second, Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix actually represent different investment theses. The bet on Samsung is that "integrated memory-plus-logic delivery" becomes the decisive factor in AI hardware. The bet on SK Hynix is that having the authority to define memory architecture is worth more than any single generation's market share — reflected in its proposal of a tiered-memory framework, its joint OCP standard with SanDisk, and its vision for CPO-connected memory pools. The bet on Micron is that memory's valuation multiple gets re-rated as the industry's cyclicality declines.

Third, I overlooked capital returns to shareholders as a positive factor when I first built these positions — I missed the point that "a company's biggest buyer can be itself." Recently SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron have all announced large-scale shareholder-return plans one after another: SK Hynix is retiring ₩40 trillion of share capital, Samsung is returning ₩100–110 trillion to shareholders, and Micron plans to start returning 100% of excess cash to shareholders starting next quarter. Over the long run, all three will return a substantial share of their excess cash, which is very supportive for rebuilding their valuation models.

Finally, memory companies are undergoing a fundamental transformation — moving from selling standardized products, to selling customized products, and eventually to selling an entire memory architecture and orchestration layer. That means the individual memory companies themselves are becoming harder and harder to substitute for one another, since their ties to the big tech giants deepen as the degree of customization deepens.

This last point is really the core of the core: going forward, the moat of a memory company can no longer be judged solely on surface-level metrics like HBM share, yield, or DRAM revenue. It will increasingly depend on whether that company has built a superior full ecosystem, and whether it can lock in a deeper degree of integration with its largest customers.

• ☐Whether CXMT's bit shipment growth exceeds market expectations
  • ☐Whether Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix's shareholder-return plans proceed as planned, and whether they keep expanding shareholder returns going forward
  • ☐Whether Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix can keep building out their own memory ecosystems and lock in a deeply integrated, "symbiotic" relationship with their customers
  • ☐

1. CXMT's bit shipment growth accelerates faster than the market expects
  2. Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix's shareholder-return plans fail to proceed as planned, or fail to keep expanding shareholder returns going forward
  3. Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix fail to build their own memory ecosystems and remain traditional commodity suppliers
What this means for my positioning

Memory is the most visible and quantifiable source of incremental growth right now, so when the market is divided on it, that's exactly when I should be willing to size up and hold with conviction. The latest changes at memory companies are fundamentally about escaping their traditional commodity status and building an entirely new ecosystem around memory. Over the long run, this could very plausibly change both the commodity nature of memory itself and the valuation logic applied to memory companies — which only strengthens my conviction to keep holding.
